content.text: Your tools are set up. Now comes the part that makes it real: telling the world, taking your first customers, and building a business that keeps going month after month. That's what the Launch Pad is for.
How the Launch Pad works
Part 1, Launch:
six lessons over about 30 days. You'll pick a launch date, shape a launch offer, tell the people who already know you, run a launch week, and look after your first customers.
Part 2, Keep Going:
five lessons for your second to sixth months: a monthly rhythm, testimonials, partnerships, raising your prices, and protecting your energy.
Monthly Deep Dive:
a new lesson on one topic every month, such as paid ads, Pinterest or selling to businesses, with a live Q&A at that month's Studio Desk session.
These lessons are the same for every path. Where launching looks different for your path, you'll find a short "For your path" note.
Your weekly check-ins
In the Launch Pad space, every week:
Monday:
"This week I will..." Post one to three things you'll do. Writing them where others can see them makes you far more likely to do them.
Friday:
Wins. Share what happened, big or small. A first enquiry counts. So does finally pressing "publish."
"I'm Open!":
when you launch, post it. Your sisters will cheer and share.
Patricia reads and replies to every check-in.
Practise here first

If you're building a community in your own business, such as a paid group, a membership or an online class, be an active member here. Post, reply, welcome new members, cheer others on. You'll build the muscle you need to run your own community, and you'll see from the inside what makes a community feel warm and worth paying for. Even if community isn't part of your plan, the women here are your first cheerleaders, collaborators and referrers.
Your action step:
Post your first Monday check-in: your path, your offer in one sentence, and the date you're aiming to launch.
Your worksheet: My Launch Pad Start
Write your answers in your notebook or the worksheet, and keep them with your Launch Plan.

A business without a launch date tends to stay "almost ready" forever. There's always one more thing to tweak. A date on the calendar turns "someday" into "the 15th," and everything else lines up behind it. Today you'll choose your date and map out the 30 days that lead to it.
What "launched" means for you
Launching doesn't mean a big splashy event. It means the day you start asking people to buy. For your path:
Social selling and services:
your offer is bookable and you announce it.
Affiliate:
your link page and first three recommendation pieces are live and shared.
Reselling:
your first 20 listings are up and you announce your shop.
Hobby business:
your shop opens, or your first market or class is booked and announced.
Building bigger:
your website and first program are live and open for enrolment.
Choose your date

Pick a date three to five weeks from today. Close enough to feel real, far enough to prepare. Avoid long weekends and major holidays (unless you sell gifts). Write it down, put it in your calendar, and tell someone.
Work backwards: your 30-day plan
Week 1 (this lesson and L2):
finish anything left from The Studio. Shape your launch offer.
Week 2 (L3):
make your warm list and send personal messages.
Week 3 (L4):
plan and schedule your launch week posts and emails.
Week 4, launch week:
share every day, reply to everyone, and welcome your first customers (L5).
After launch (L6):
look at what worked.
Fit it to the hours in your Launch Plan. If you have five hours a week, plan five hours a week, not twenty. Small and steady beats a burst you can't keep up.
"Ready enough" beats ready

You'll want to delay. That's normal, and it's usually fear dressed up as perfectionism. Your first customers won't notice the font you agonized over. They'll notice that you showed up and helped them. You can improve everything after launch, with real feedback.
Example (not a real member):

Carol picked a date four weeks out, the first Tuesday of the month. She blocked Tuesday and Thursday mornings for launch work and told her Facebook group she'd be opening her Paperwork Planning Sessions that day. Telling them made it real.
Your action step:
Choose your launch date, write what "launched" means for you, map your four weeks into your calendar, and post your date in the Monday check-in.
Your worksheet: My 30-Day Launch Plan
Write your answers in your notebook or the worksheet, and keep them with your Launch Plan.

People who've been meaning to buy from you often need one small reason to do it now rather than "one day." A launch offer gives them that reason, honestly. Today you'll shape yours.
The three parts of a good launch offer
A founding price or bonus.
A lower price for your first customers, or something extra at the regular price: a bonus session, a free gift with the first order, early access.
A real deadline.
"Until Sunday, June 8" or "for the first ten people." It must be true: when the deadline passes, the offer ends.
A clear reason.
"I'm opening my doors and want my first clients to get the best deal while I collect feedback." People like being part of something new.
Keep it honest
Fake urgency ("only 2 left!" when there are 50) damages trust and, in Canada and the US, can break advertising law. You never need it. A real founding price and a real date are persuasive enough.
How much of a discount?

Enough to feel worth acting on, not so much that you resent the work. Many women choose 15% to 25% off, or a bonus worth about that much. Remember the fees and your hourly rate from your Money Plan: you should still be paid fairly.
Ask for something in return

Founding customers are perfect people to ask for feedback and, if they're happy, a testimonial. Tell them up front: "In return for the founding price, I'll ask for your honest feedback afterwards." Most people are glad to help.
For your path
Services:
a founding price for the first five or ten clients.
Hobby business:
a launch-day bonus (a free gift tag, free local delivery) or a market-day special.
Affiliate:
no discount needed; your "launch" is your best recommendation content, shared widely.
Reselling:
a launch-weekend bundle or free shipping on your first orders.
Building bigger:
a founding group at a lower price, with the promise they'll help shape the program.
Example (not a real member):
Gwen's launch offer: anyone who orders a table runner in her first week gets free local delivery and a matching set of coasters. It ended at midnight on Sunday, and she said so in every post.
Your action step:
Write your launch offer: the price or bonus, the deadline, the reason, and what you'll ask for in return. Share it in the Monday check-in for feedback.
Your worksheet: My Launch Offer
Write your answers in your notebook or the worksheet, and keep them with your Launch Plan.
My founding price or bonus:
My deadline (a date or a number of spots):
My reason, in one sentence:
What I'll ask founding customers for (feedback, a testimonial):
After fees, what I keep from each sale at the founding price:
Share in The Lounge
Share your launch offer in one or two sentences. Sisters, would it make you act this week?

Here's the secret most launch advice skips: your first customers almost always come from people who already know you, or from people they tell. You've spent decades building relationships: former colleagues, neighbours, church and club friends, family, the women from your book club. That's your warm circle, and it's one of the biggest advantages of starting a business in this chapter of life.
Step 1: Make your list (20 to 50 names)

Write down everyone who might buy, or who knows people who might. Go through your phone contacts, your Facebook friends, your holiday card list. Don't judge yet; just write. Next to each name, note how you know them.
Step 2: Write personal messages, not announcements
A personal message gets replies. A group announcement gets scrolled past. Send each person a short note in your own words, by text, email or private message:

"Hi Margaret! I've started something new and you're one of the first people I wanted to tell. I'm now helping women caring for ageing parents get their paperwork sorted, in a one-hour session. I open on the 15th, with a founding price for my first ten clients. Would you, or anyone you know, find this helpful? I'd love it if you passed it on."
Notice what it does: it's personal, it says what you do and who it's for, it mentions the launch offer, and it makes two easy asks: "is this for you?" and "do you know someone?"
Step 3: Ask for the share, not just the sale
Many people on your list won't need what you sell. But they know someone who does. "Would you pass this on?" is easy to say yes to, and it's how warm circles grow.
Step 4: Follow up once, kindly
If someone doesn't reply in a week, one gentle follow-up is fine: "Just checking you saw my note. No pressure at all!" Then let it go.
What about my email list?

Personal one-to-one messages to people you know are fine. But don't add your warm circle to your email list without asking first. Instead, invite them: "Would you like me to add you to my monthly email?" It respects them, and it keeps you inside Canada's anti-spam law (and the US equivalent).
It might feel awkward. Do it anyway
Many women feel they're "bothering" people. You're not. You're offering something useful, and people who care about you want to know what you're doing. Most will be delighted.
Example (not a real member):
Diane wrote a list of 42 former colleagues and friends and sent eight personal messages a day for a week. Nineteen replied, four booked a founding coaching package, and six passed her name on.
Your action step:
Write your list of 20 to 50 names and send your first ten personal messages this week.
Your worksheet: My Warm Circle
Write your answers in your notebook or the worksheet, and keep them with your Launch Plan.

Launch week is when you show up more than usual. People need to hear about something several times before they act, and most won't see every post. So for one week you'll share a little every day, each time from a different angle. Today you'll plan and schedule the whole week.
Five angles for five days
Your story (launch day):
why you started this, who it's for, and that you're open. "After 30 years running an office, and sorting out my own mum's paperwork, I'm opening..."
The problem:
describe the situation your customer is in, in her own words (from your Idea Test). Let her feel understood.
The offer:
exactly what she gets, the price, the founding bonus, and how to book or buy.
Proof:
a story from someone you've helped, a photo of your work, a kind comment from your Idea Test (with permission), or simply your experience.
The last call (deadline day):
"The founding price ends at midnight tonight." This is often your busiest day.
On days six and seven, thank everyone, share a behind-the-scenes photo, and answer questions.
Where to share
Your one platform
(from The Studio): one post a day.
Your email list:
three emails: launch day, the offer, and the last call. Many sales come from the last-call email.
Your Facebook groups:
only where the rules allow, and helpfully.
Your warm circle:
a personal message to anyone who said "tell me when you open."
The Launch Pad:
post your "I'm Open!" so your sisters can share.
Write it all before the week starts

In the week before launch, write every post and email, make your images in Canva, and schedule them (Meta Business Suite for Facebook and Instagram, and your email tool for emails). Then during launch week your job is simple: show up, reply to every comment and message quickly, and welcome customers.
For your path
Hobby business at a market:
your launch week is the week before the market. Post your table preview, a product each day, and "find me at..." on the day.
Affiliate:
share one of your best recommendation pieces each day.
Building bigger:
add a short free live session ("Ask me anything about...") mid-week. Live events bring people from interested to ready.
Example (not a real member):

Linda scheduled five pins and five Facebook posts the weekend before her shop launch, plus three emails. During the week she spent 20 minutes a day replying to comments. She sold 14 items in her first seven days.
Your action step:
Write and schedule your five posts and three emails, and plan your "I'm Open!" post.

Write your answers in your notebook or the worksheet, and keep them with your Launch Plan.

Your first customers are precious. Look after them beautifully and they become your testimonials, your referrals and often your repeat customers. Today you'll set up how you welcome them, deliver to them and follow up.
Step 1: The welcome (within 24 hours)

The moment someone pays is when she's most excited and most unsure. Within a day, send a warm welcome that tells her exactly what happens next: the date, the time, the link or address, what to bring or prepare, and how to reach you. If your tools can send it automatically (Lesson D4), add a short personal note as well.
Step 2: Deliver a little more than promised

Not a lot more, just a thoughtful touch: a handwritten note in the parcel, a short summary emailed after a session, a follow-up tip a week later. Small surprises are what people tell their friends about.
Step 3: Ask how it went
A few days after delivery, ask two simple questions:
"What was the most helpful part?"
"Is there anything I could have done better?"
The answers improve your offer, and the first answer is often your testimonial in the making.
Step 4: Ask for a testimonial (with permission)

If she's happy, ask: "Would you be willing to let me share what you said? I can use your first name and town, or keep it anonymous." Always get a clear yes before sharing anything, and keep her words exactly as she wrote them. Lesson L8 goes deeper.
Step 5: Ask for a referral
"Do you know anyone else who'd find this helpful?" Happy customers love to help, but they rarely think to unless you ask. Make it easy: give them a link or a card to pass on.
Keep a record
Add every customer to your client tracker or money tracker: what they bought, when, what they said, and whether you've asked for a testimonial and a referral.
For your path
Hobby business and reselling:
pack every order carefully, include a thank-you card with your shop link, and ship when you said you would.
Affiliate:
your "customers" are your readers. Reply to every comment and question; that's where trust grows.
Example (not a real member):

After each Paperwork Planning Session, Carol emails a one-page summary and the checklist she promised, plus a link to a free document-folder template. Three of her first five clients sent her friends.
Your action step:
Write your welcome message, choose your "little more," and write your follow-up message with the two questions and the testimonial and referral asks.
Your worksheet: My First Customers
Write your answers in your notebook or the worksheet, and keep them with your Launch Plan.

You launched. Whatever the numbers say, take a moment: you did something most people only talk about. Now, while it's fresh, look at what happened. Your launch is the best market research you'll ever get, because it's real people making real decisions with real money.
Step 1: Gather your numbers
How many people saw your launch (rough post views, email opens)
How many enquired or clicked
How many bought, and at what price
Total money in, and total money out (fees, materials, any costs)
Hours you spent
Your money tracker, your email tool and your platform's insights have most of this.
Step 2: Where did your customers come from?

For each customer, note where they found you: your warm circle, a Facebook group, your email, a referral, a market, a search. Almost always, one or two sources brought most of the sales. That's where to put more of your time.
Step 3: What did people say?

Read back over the questions, replies and comments. What did people ask about most? What made them hesitate? What did they love? This tells you what to explain more clearly, what to change, and sometimes what your next offer should be.
Step 4: Three questions
What worked?
Keep doing it.
What didn't?
Drop it or change it.
What's one thing to change next month?
Just one. Small changes, kept up, add up.
If the launch was quieter than you hoped

That's common, and it isn't failure. It's information. Usually the cause is one of three things: not enough people saw it (share more widely and for longer), the offer wasn't clear (simplify how you describe it), or it wasn't quite what people wanted (look at what they asked about instead). Bring your numbers to the Studio Desk session and we'll look at them together.
Example (not a real member):

Gwen's launch brought nine sales: six from her craft fair, two from Etsy, and one from her email list. People kept asking whether she did custom colours. Her one change: a "choose your colours" option at a higher price.
Your action step:
Gather your numbers, find where your customers came from, answer the three questions, and share your one change in the Friday wins thread.
Your worksheet: My Launch Review
Write your answers in your notebook or the worksheet, and keep them with your Launch Plan.

A launch is a sprint. A business is a walk you take every week. After launch, many women either stop (because the excitement fades) or try to keep launch-week pace (and burn out). The answer is a simple monthly rhythm: the same few things, at the same times, every month. Today you'll set yours.
The four parts of a monthly rhythm
Showing up (weekly).
Your content routine from The Studio: a set number of posts each week, batched in one sitting, plus ten minutes a day of replying and connecting.
Staying in touch (monthly).
One email to your list: one helpful thing, one personal thing, one invitation.
Selling on purpose (monthly).
One clear invitation each month. It might be a reminder of your offer, a monthly special, a new class date or a seasonal product. If you never ask, people assume you're busy or closed.
Looking at the numbers (monthly).
Your money date (Lesson S4), plus 10 minutes on what worked: where did customers come from this month?
Put it in your calendar, once
Turn the rhythm into repeating calendar events. For example:
Monday morning: batch this week's posts (1 hour)
Every weekday: 10 minutes of replies
First Sunday of the month: money date and numbers review (30 minutes)
Second Tuesday: write and send the monthly email (1 hour)
Third week: this month's invitation goes out
Now you don't have to decide what to do each week. You just follow the calendar.
Plan your year loosely

Mark the seasons that matter to your business: holidays, gift seasons, back to school, tax time, wedding season, market season. Plan your monthly invitation around them. (The Monthly Deep Dive on holiday and seasonal selling goes deeper.)
Example (not a real member):

Diane's rhythm: two posts a week written on Monday, a newsletter on the second Tuesday, and a monthly free "career clarity" call that leads to her coaching package. It takes her about four hours a week, matching the hours in her Launch Plan.
Your action step:
Write your monthly rhythm, put it in your calendar as repeating events, and mark the key seasons for your business on a 12-month calendar.
Your worksheet: My Monthly Rhythm
Write your answers in your notebook or the worksheet, and keep them with your Launch Plan.

When people are deciding whether to buy, what other customers say matters more than anything you say about yourself. A few honest testimonials can do more for your business than any amount of clever wording. Today you'll set up a simple, honest way to collect them, and learn the rules that keep you safe.
Step 1: Ask at the right moment

The best time is right after a good result: the session that helped, the order that arrived beautifully, the class she loved. Use the follow-up from Lesson L5. When she says something kind, ask: "Would you be willing to let me share that?"
Step 2: Make it easy
Offer three simple prompts she can answer in a sentence or two:
What was going on before you came to me?
What did we do together (or what did you buy)?
What's different now?
Those three answers make a testimonial that tells a story.
Step 3: Always get permission, and keep her words

Ask how she'd like to be named: full name, first name and town, initials, or anonymous. Keep her words as she wrote them. You can shorten, but never change the meaning or add words she didn't say. Keep the permission (an email or message is fine) in your Customers folder.
Step 4: Google and other reviews

If you have a Google Business Profile (Lesson C6) or an Etsy shop, reviews there help new people find you. Ask every customer the same way, whether you think she was delighted or not. Google doesn't allow businesses to ask only happy customers, or to offer anything in return for a review.
The rules, in plain words
Never write fake reviews

, or have friends or family review you as if they were customers. In Canada, the Competition Bureau treats fake reviews as misleading advertising. In the US, the FTC's 2024 rule bans fake reviews and testimonials outright.
Never pay or reward people for positive reviews.
No discounts, gifts or entries into a draw in exchange.
Don't hide or bully away honest negative reviews.
Reply politely and offer to make it right. A calm reply to a complaint often wins more trust than ten five-star reviews.
Use AI to tidy your own words, never to write a customer's.
Where to use them
On your website (home page and offer page), in your launch and monthly posts, in your welcome emails, beside your prices, and on your market table as a small printed card.
Example (not a real member):

Carol's favourite testimonial, used with permission: "I'd been putting off Mum's paperwork for a year. In one hour with Carol, I knew exactly what was missing and what to do first. I slept that night. — Janet, White Rock."
Your action step:
Write your testimonial request with the three prompts, send it to your first customers, and put your first testimonial on your website or profile.

Other businesses already have the trust of the people you want to reach. Partnering with them is one of the fastest, kindest ways to grow: you help each other's customers, and both businesses benefit. Today you'll find two possible partners and suggest one simple idea.
Who makes a good partner?
Someone who serves the same people as you, but doesn't sell the same thing. Ask: "Before or after my customer buys from me, who else does she go to?"
Carol (caregiver paperwork) partners with a mobile hairdresser for seniors, a seniors' moving service and an estate lawyer.
Gwen (quilting) partners with the local fabric shop, a cafe that hosts her classes and a gift shop.
Diane (career coaching) partners with a resume writer, a financial planner and a women's networking group.
Five simple ways to work together
Referral swap:
you recommend each other to customers who need what the other does.
Guest spot:
you speak at her event or write for her newsletter, and she does the same for you.
Shared workshop:
"Downsizing With Peace of Mind", run together, each covering your part.
Bundle or gift box:
your products together, sold by one or both of you.
Space sharing:
a shop hosts your class, a cafe displays your work.
How to approach a partner
Start by being useful, not by asking. Follow her, buy from her, recommend her. Then send a short, specific note:

"Hi Maureen, I love how you help families with downsizing. I run paperwork planning sessions for women caring for ageing parents, and many of my clients are about to move a parent. Would you be open to a coffee to see if we could refer to each other, or run a joint evening at the library?"
Keep the first ask small. A coffee is easier to say yes to than a big project.
Agree the basics in writing
For anything more than a casual referral, write down who does what, who pays for what, how money is shared, and the dates. An email you both reply "agreed" to is enough for small projects.
Don't forget your sisters
The women in this community are natural partners. Post in The Lounge what kind of partner you're looking for. Someone here may serve the same customers from a different angle.
Example (not a real member):

Gwen asked her local fabric shop whether she could run her beginners' class there. The shop provides the room for free; students get 10% off fabric on the day. Her class fills every time, and the shop sells more fabric.
Your action step:
List five possible partners, choose two, become useful to them, and send one short, specific note suggesting a coffee and one idea.
Your worksheet: My Partners
Write your answers in your notebook or the worksheet, and keep them with your Launch Plan.

Most women start by charging too little. That's understandable: you were building confidence and testing your idea. But a price that's too low wears you out and makes it hard to keep going. Today you'll look at whether it's time to raise your prices, and whether a second offer could serve the people you already have.
Signs it's time to raise your prices
You're booked up, or selling out, most months
Customers say "that's a great deal" (it means it's cheap)
Your hourly earnings are below your Launch Plan goal (Lesson C5 and your Money Plan)
Your costs have gone up
You feel a little resentful doing the work at that price
Two or more of these? It's time.
How to raise prices gracefully
Founding prices end as promised.
Your launch offer had a deadline; now the regular price begins.
Raise for new customers first.
Existing customers can keep their price for a while, as a thank-you.
Give notice.
"From March 1, my sessions will be $120. Book before then at the current price." This often brings a rush of bookings.
Don't apologize.
One simple sentence is enough. People expect prices to rise.
Raise in steps.
10% to 20% at a time is easier for you and your customers.
Adding a second offer
The easiest sale is to someone who already bought and loved it. Ask: "What do my customers need next?"
A step up:
a package of sessions instead of one; a larger or custom version of your product.
A step down:
a lower-priced way in, such as a guide, a group class or a smaller item, for people not ready for your main offer.
A repeat:
something they come back for, such as a monthly membership, a refill, a seasonal collection or a follow-up session.

Use what customers asked about in your launch review (Lesson L6). Their questions often point straight to your next offer. Test it with a few people before building it out, just as you did in Tutorials Lesson 19.
Example (not a real member):

Carol was fully booked at $95 a session for two months running. She raised her price to $125 for new clients with a month's notice, and added a $295 "Peace of Mind Package": three sessions plus a finished document binder. A third of her clients now choose the package.
Your action step:
Check your signs, decide on your new price and when it starts, write your one-sentence announcement, and sketch one second offer to test.
Your worksheet: My Prices and Next Offer
Write your answers in your notebook or the worksheet, and keep them with your Launch Plan.

Many of us came to this chapter to get away from work that drained us. It would be a sad irony if the business built to give us freedom became a new exhausting job. Growing well means growing at a pace you can enjoy for years. Today you'll put some protection in place.
Go back to your Life Picture

In Tutorials Lesson 5 you pictured the life your business would fund: the trips, the garden, the grandchildren, the mornings that are your own. Read it again. Is your business serving that picture, or eating into it?
Guard your hours

Your Launch Plan set the hours you wanted to work. Check your calendar from the last month. Are you inside them? If not, something has to give: raise prices (Lesson L10), drop the work that earns least, or get help (Lesson D7). Working more hours is the last answer, not the first.
Learn to say no, kindly
Every yes to something that isn't right is a no to something that is. Some things worth saying no to:
Customers who aren't a fit, or who want a discount every time
"Can I just pick your brain?" requests that take an hour (offer your paid session instead)
Custom requests that take twice as long for the same price
Opportunities that sound exciting but don't fit your plan
A kind, simple no: "Thank you for thinking of me. That's not something I'm taking on right now."
Set boundaries your customers can see

Your working hours, how quickly you reply ("within one business day"), your cancellation policy, and what's included. Put them in your welcome message and on your website. Clear boundaries make customers feel looked after, not turned away.
Build in rest

Put time off in your calendar first: holidays, a quiet week after a busy season, one full day a week with no business at all. Use your email tool's out-of-office message and pause your posts. Your business will survive a week without you. It's better for it.
Notice the warning signs

Dreading your work, putting off customer messages, feeling resentful, sleeping badly, no time for the things your business was meant to fund. If you notice them, slow down and talk to someone: your sisters in the Launch Pad, or us at Studio Desk.
Example (not a real member):

Gwen said yes to every custom order in her first busy season and found herself sewing until midnight. Now she takes six custom orders a month, at a higher price, and keeps Sundays for her grandchildren.
Your action step:
Reread your Life Picture, check last month's hours against your plan, write your boundaries, write your kind no, and put your next week off in your calendar.
Your worksheet: Protecting My Energy
Write your answers in your notebook or the worksheet, and keep them with your Launch Plan.

lp.name: Monthly Deep Dive: Paid Ads, Carefully

content.text: Paid ads can bring your business to people who'd never otherwise find you. They can also eat money fast if you start too soon. This month's Deep Dive is about doing it carefully: when you're ready, how to test with a small budget, and how to tell whether it's working. Bring your questions to this month's Studio Desk session.
Are you ready? Three checks
Your offer already sells without ads.
You've had customers from your warm circle, posts or markets. Ads amplify what works; they don't fix an offer people don't want.
You know your numbers.
What a customer is worth to you (the profit from a first sale, and from repeat sales).
You have money you can afford to lose.
Treat your first ad budget as tuition. If losing it would worry you, wait.
If any answer is no, keep building with free methods for now. That's not a failure; it's good business.
Start with Facebook and Instagram
Meta (which runs both) lets you choose who sees your ad by location, age and interests, which suits local and niche businesses. Two ways in:
Boost a post:
the simplest. Pick a post that already did well, press "Boost," choose your area, budget and days.
Meta Ads Manager:
more control, more settings. Worth learning once boosting works for you.
Or let AI do the heavy lifting: Zeely

Zeely uses AI to create ad images and videos and run them on Facebook and Instagram for you. We use it. Plans start at about $30 a month, plus the money you spend on the ads themselves, and Zeely can add a percentage on top of your ad spend, so read its current pricing before you start.
Your first test
One goal:
for example, messages, bookings or visits to your sign-up page. Not all at once.
One audience:
people within 25 km of you, for instance, or women 50 and over interested in gardening.
One or two ads:
your best post, a clear photo, and one clear next step.
A small, set budget:
for a local awareness test, $10 to $25 a day for seven days is a common starting point. Set a total limit so you can't overspend.
Don't touch it for a week.
Ads need a few days to settle.
Did it work?

Divide what you spent by what you got: cost per message, per sign-up or per sale. Compare it with what a customer is worth. If a $150 test brought three customers worth $100 profit each, that's worth repeating. If it brought likes but no customers, change one thing (the photo, the words, or the audience) and test again, or go back to free methods.
Watch out for scams

Once you advertise, you may get messages claiming your ad account is about to be shut down, with a link to "verify." Meta won't contact you through Messenger like that. Never click; go to Meta Business Suite yourself to check.
Example (not a real member):

Gwen boosted her best-performing post (a photo of her Christmas runners) to women within 30 km for seven days at $15 a day. The $105 test brought 41 visits to her Etsy shop and five sales. She'll run it again next November.
Your action step:
Do the three readiness checks. If you're ready, plan one small test (goal, audience, ad, budget, dates). If you're not, write down what needs to happen first.
Your worksheet: My Ad Test
Write your answers in your notebook or the worksheet, and keep them with your Launch Plan.
